prompt: Which gets a bigger share of its electricity from clean sources?
insight: Switzerland runs on Alpine hydro plus nuclear and is effectively fossil-free. Austria has the same mountains but no reactors, so gas fills its winter gaps.

prompt: Which gets a bigger share of its electricity from clean sources?
insight: Both lean on nuclear, but Slovakia leans harder and adds Danube hydro on top. Belgium's long-running phase-out politics keep pulling its share down.

prompt: Which gets a bigger share of its electricity from clean sources?
insight: Kenya runs on Rift Valley geothermal plus hydro and wind, giving it one of the cleanest grids on earth. Clean electricity is not a rich-country privilege.

prompt: Which gets a bigger share of its electricity from clean sources?
insight: Britain's coal-to-wind switch is one of the fastest grid decarbonisations ever recorded. Spain got further still, using solar and hydro Britain simply doesn't have.

prompt: Which gets a bigger share of its electricity from clean sources?
insight: Greece went from lignite-dominated to majority-clean in about fifteen years. The US has more clean generation than any country except China, and still a dirtier average.

prompt: Which gets a bigger share of its electricity from coal?
insight: Germany takes the criticism for coal; Australia quietly runs on twice as much of it, and exports more of it than almost any country on earth.

prompt: Which gets a bigger share of its electricity from coal?
insight: Poland's grid was built on domestic hard coal and lignite, and mining employment has made retiring it politically expensive. Australia is on a similar path, a few years further along.

prompt: Which gets a bigger share of its electricity from coal?
insight: China burns far more coal than India in absolute terms, yet has also built more wind, solar and hydro than anyone. India's grid is the more coal-dependent of the two.

prompt: Which gets a bigger share of its electricity from coal?
insight: Russia is a fossil fuel superpower that burns gas rather than coal at home - it has more gas than it can profitably sell. Germany still leans on lignite it can dig up domestically.

prompt: Which gets a bigger share of its electricity from coal?
insight: Taiwan has been phasing out nuclear while electricity demand from chip fabrication climbs. Coal and gas filled the gap. South Korea kept its reactors.

prompt: Whose electricity produces more CO2?
insight: Australia and Canada have similar populations and similar wealth. Canada's grid is hydro and nuclear, Australia's is still substantially coal - same conditions, opposite outcome.

prompt: Whose electricity produces more CO2?
insight: Poland has roughly a fifth of Brazil's population and higher power sector emissions. Brazil's hydro-heavy grid is the entire difference.

prompt: Whose electricity produces more CO2?
insight: France's whole grid, serving 68 million people, emits less carbon than Singapore's, serving under 6 million. Nuclear and hydro are the reason.

prompt: Whose electricity produces more CO2?
insight: South Africa's grid is almost entirely coal, run by a single struggling utility. Vietnam is growing fast but has added serious solar alongside its coal.

prompt: Which generates more electricity per person?
insight: Canada generates more electricity per person than the US: cold winters, heavy industry, and hydro cheap enough to make electric heating the rational choice.

prompt: Which generates more electricity per person?
insight: Kuwait's air conditioning and seawater desalination run on heavily subsidised domestic gas. Cheap energy always gets used, whatever the climate demands.

prompt: Which generates more electricity per person?
insight: China now generates more electricity per person than Spain. No single number captures how far its industrialisation has run more clearly than this one.

prompt: Which generates more electricity per person?
insight: Sweden generates nearly three times Germany's electricity per person. Abundant hydro and nuclear made power cheap enough to electrify heating and heavy industry.

prompt: Which generates more electricity per person?
insight: Japan out-generates the Netherlands per person despite a decade of hard-won post-Fukushima efficiency gains. Industrial structure sets the floor.

prompt: Which generates more electricity per person?
insight: Both are dense, rich and urban. South Korea's steel, shipbuilding and semiconductor plants push it above Singapore's services-and-trade economy.

prompt: Which is more energy independent?
insight: Austrian Alpine hydro needs no fuel at all. India burns a great deal of coal but digs most of it up itself, which is why it scores better here than its emissions would suggest.

prompt: Which is more energy independent?
insight: Denmark's wind fleet needs no fuel deliveries, which is exactly what this score rewards. Germany still buys gas and hard coal from abroad.

prompt: Which is more energy independent?
insight: France's reactors sit on French soil, but France mines no uranium at all - every fuel rod is imported. Independence is about where the fuel comes from, not where the plant stands.

prompt: Which is more energy independent?
insight: Japan imports almost all its fossil fuel and shut most of its reactors after Fukushima, leaving it among the most import-exposed developed economies.

prompt: Which is more energy independent?
insight: Nigeria runs its grid on its own gas and hydro, so on paper it imports nothing. This score measures import exposure, not reliability - Nigerian supply still fails constantly.

prompt: Which gets a bigger share of its electricity from nuclear?
insight: Slovakia draws two thirds of its electricity from nuclear, among the highest shares in the world. Belgium has been legislating a nuclear phase-out since 2003 and postponing it ever since.

prompt: Which gets a bigger share of its electricity from nuclear?
insight: Sweden closed four reactors in the 2010s and has since reversed course politically. Czechia never wavered, and now leans on nuclear harder than Sweden does.

prompt: Which gets a bigger share of its electricity from nuclear?
insight: Britain opened the world's first commercial nuclear plant in 1956, and most of that fleet has since retired. Spain's newer reactors now carry the bigger share.

prompt: Which gets a bigger share of its electricity from nuclear?
insight: Finland's Olkiluoto 3 took some seventeen years to build, but a single reactor was enough to visibly shift a small country's entire electricity mix.

prompt: Which gets a bigger share of its electricity from nuclear?
insight: The US operates far more reactors than South Korea, but its grid is so much bigger that nuclear's share comes out smaller. Absolute size and share routinely tell opposite stories.

prompt: Which gets a bigger share of its electricity from nuclear?
insight: Even through a full-scale invasion, Ukraine ran most of its grid on nuclear. Reactors are hard to build, and equally hard to replace once you depend on them.

prompt: Which generates more solar power?
insight: Chile's Atacama desert is the sunniest place on earth and most of its solar fleet sits there. Britain gets a comparable total from a country with a fraction of the sunlight.

prompt: Which generates more solar power?
insight: Cloudy Germany out-solars sunny France by almost 3x. Sunlight was never the constraint; installed panels are.

prompt: Which generates more solar power?
insight: Italy produces well over twice Britain's solar power. Rooftop subsidies in the 2010s, not latitude, opened the gap.

prompt: Which generates more solar power?
insight: The Netherlands generates more solar power than Pakistan, a country with ten times the population and far more sun. Access to capital, not climate, sets the pace.

prompt: Which generates more electricity in total?
insight: Turkey overtook Britain and keeps pulling away. British electricity demand has been flat or falling since 2005 as industry shrank and efficiency improved.

prompt: Which generates more electricity in total?
insight: Russia out-generates Japan. Cheap domestic gas and an energy-intensive heavy industry base make electricity worth using in ways it simply isn't in Japan.

prompt: Which generates more electricity in total?
insight: Malaysia out-generates Poland from a similar population. Southeast Asian electricity demand is growing at rates Europe last saw in the 1960s.

prompt: Which generates more electricity in total?
insight: Thailand out-generates Poland. The centre of gravity in global electricity has moved decisively to Asia, and it is still moving.

prompt: Which generates more wind power?
insight: Sweden generates more wind power than Australia with about a third of the population. Australia's renewable build leaned into rooftop solar instead, where it leads the world.

prompt: Which generates more wind power?
insight: Germany still leads on total output, but Brazil's northeastern trade winds are among the steadiest on earth, so each Brazilian turbine earns far more than a German one.

prompt: Which generates more wind power?
insight: Brazil out-produces India on wind with a fifth of the population. Its northeastern coast has unusually constant trade winds, which lifts output per turbine dramatically.

prompt: Which generates more wind power?
insight: Spain has been a wind pioneer since the 1990s. Canada has far more windy land and far fewer people on it - geography alone doesn't build turbines.

prompt: Which generates more wind power?
insight: Britain built the world's largest offshore wind fleet while France bet on nuclear. Both are low-carbon strategies; they just look nothing alike.

prompt: Which gets a bigger share of its electricity from clean sources?
insight: Both grids were built on big hydro. Brazil added wind and solar on top; Canada's remaining fossil generation is concentrated in Alberta and Saskatchewan.

prompt: Which gets a bigger share of its electricity from coal?
insight: Both grids run on domestic coal. India's is the more dependent, and it is also the fastest-growing large electricity market in the world.

prompt: Whose electricity produces more CO2?
insight: Japan's power sector emits roughly triple Germany's, largely because the reactors idled after Fukushima were backfilled with coal and gas.

prompt: Which generates more electricity per person?
insight: Norway generates more than twice as much electricity per person as the US. Near-free hydro attracted aluminium smelters and made electrifying everything else the default.

prompt: Which generates more solar power?
insight: Germany still out-produces Spain on solar with roughly half the sunshine. It started twenty years earlier and never stopped installing.

prompt: Which generates more solar power?
insight: Spain wins on raw output, but the Netherlands is one of Europe's cloudiest countries and lands in the same league. Panel count beats sunshine hours.

prompt: Which generates more solar power?
insight: India passed Japan on solar roughly a decade after starting seriously. Solar is now the cheapest new power in most of the world, so it scales fastest where demand is still growing.

prompt: Which generates more electricity in total?
insight: Japan generates more electricity from 125 million people than Brazil does from 215 million. Wealth and industry drive electricity use far harder than headcount.

prompt: Which generates more electricity in total?
insight: France's nuclear fleet gives it one of Europe's largest grids and makes it a net exporter to its neighbours in most years.

prompt: Which generates more wind power?
insight: Denmark invented the modern wind industry and gets a larger share of its power from wind than any country on earth. It is also small, so its total output is easily beaten.
